newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. to initiate big Internet service.
newsitem.headline: U.N. to initiate big Internet service.

text.p: The United Nations said on Monday it was initiating a vast Internet service expected to contain 270,000 documents in six languages by December in an effort to drag itself into the 21st century.

"You can call up and find out what the most recent thing that happened in the Security Council or you can ask about rainfall and it is there," said Joseph Connor, undersecretary-general for administration and management.

He said the United Nations got about 200,000 requests a week and had already begun using the Internet to answer them. "We couldn't respond without the Internet," said Connor, an American and the former chief executive of the Price-Waterhouse accounting firm.

Connor, at the behest of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, undertook a large efficiency project that has cut about $254 million from the secretariat budget, frozen at $2.6 billion over the two year 1996-1997 period. This included leaving 900 posts empty.

With mounds of paper still the main means of communication, Connor said it was time for bureaucracy as well as most governments in the world to change work habits. To this end he pointed to widespread travel by U.N. officials, saying much of it could be replaced by audio-visual conference hook-ups. One such meeting took place on Monday between diplomats and U.N. officials in Geneva, Vienna and New York.

"This organisation does not always consider whether travel is necessary or not," Connor told a news conference. "I told the Security Council members this morning that you don't have to wait for Mr Blix to come over on his planned trip," he said in reference to Hans Blix, the director of the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency.
"They can have him on hand anytime they want him," he added. "But you've got to get people comfortable with the methodology. It is worth pursuing and it's really is cheap."

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Madeleine Albright has vowed to veto Boutros-Ghali's reelection for another five-year term, mainly because of his alleged lack of reform projects. In a statement on Thursday, she complimented the report and Connor but took care not to mention Boutros-Ghali.
"One of the most gratifying aspects of this report is how U.N. managers and staff have demonstrated that they are both willing and able to lead in this process of change," she said.

Connor, however, has warned that the world body will be broke by the end of the year unless there is an infusion of American funds. The United States is in arrears for $1.6 billion for peacekeeping and regular dues, more than half of the total debt of the United Nations.
